questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman presented with headache and fever for 4 days. She had type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, controlled with metformin and amlodipine. There was no recent travel. She lived at home with her partner. She had previously had a rash with penicillin. Her partner reported that she had been unsteady on her feet for the last 2 days. On examination she was drowsy, with a reduced conscious level (GCS 14/15). Her temperature was 38.2°C, and her heart rate was 98 beats/minute. She had neck stiffness and was photophobic. She had nystagmus on left lateral gaze and a slight facial droop on the right. Peripheral nervous system examination was grossly intact, but difficult to assess formally as the patient was unable to follow commands.
questions.lead_in: In addition to ceftriaxone, what antibacterial agent should be given?
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole She is displaying signs of a meningoencephalitis with rhombic involvement (possible ataxia, nystagmus, and VIIth cranial nerve palsy) and is at higher risk of Listeria due to her age. Listeria are insensitive to cephalosporins. Empirical antibacterial treatment would normally consist of a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone as well as amoxicillin/ampicillin to cover for Listeria in this age group; however, as there is a history of penicillin allergy, TMP–SMX (co-trimoxazole) is used for Listeria cover instead. Another alternative would be meropenem.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q11

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida, 32+4/40 attended with a 1-day history of fever, chills, myalgia, and malaise. The pregnancy had been uncomplicated to date. She had had all her childhood vaccinations on schedule and had not been in contact with a rash illness in this pregnancy. She worked in an office. No other contacts were unwell. A single temperature measurement was 38.0°C, but otherwise there was no other abnormality. There was no meningism, no rash, and no pharyngitis. Bedside urinalysis was negative. She was kept for 6 hours’ observation during which she was afebrile. She was discharged home with advice to seek help if her symptoms persisted. Three days later, her clinician was phoned by the microbiology laboratory with the following result: Blood cultures: gram-positive rods
questions.lead_in: What are the possible consequences that should be taken into consideration?

options.text: No increased risk of adverse outcome

questions.explanation: Stillbirth This is a case of maternal listeriosis. The risks of this in late pregnancy include death in utero or premature delivery of an infected infant if the infection progresses untreated. The classic description is of a biphasic illness, in which the first phase is a nonspecific acute influenza-like illness. Blood cultures at this point are invaluable in providing an early diagnosis. If unnoticed or untreated, premature labor or death in utero may follow within 2–14 days of the acute presentation. This can be prevented by early antibiotic treatment
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q48

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of fever, headaches, nausea, and watery diarrhea. Her symptoms developed 12 hours after a picnic at which she ate pate sandwiches and salad. She was concerned as she was 6 weeks pregnant.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes The history is consistent with a diagnosis of Listeria monocytogenes gastroenteritis and although Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus can also cause infection following consumption of infected food within a short period of time, S. aureus infection presents with vomiting 1–6 hours following ingestion; fever is rare, and symptoms usually resolve within 24–48 hours. Vomiting is the predominant symptom in all the other diagnoses listed. Listeria monocytogenes is more likely to cause invasive disease in pregnant patients and can lead to possible fetal loss in severe disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q8

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man was admitted for respiratory failure, cranial nerve paralysis, and hemiplegia. He was normally well and did not take any regular medications. He had no known drug allergies. Investigations: CSF microscopy: mild pleocytosis with neutrophilic predominance CSF Gram stain: CSF/plasma glucose: normal ratio CT head: normal appearances MRI brain: diffuse brainstem encephalitis
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ampicillin Be aware of Listeria monocytogenes (gram-positive bacilli as shown in the image) rhombencephalitis (brainstempredominant encephalitis) that occurs more commonly in immunocompetent patients (as opposed to regular Listeriaassociated meningitis in immunocompromised patients). Ampicillin is the drug of choice for Listeria infection. (Image from Murray PR, Rosenthal KS, Pfaller MA. Medical Microbiology. 8th ed. Elsevier; 2016.)

questions.model_answer: a) Listeria monocytogenes (neurolisteriosis/meningoencephalitis). b) Foodborne acquisition via the gastrointestinal tract after ingestion of contaminated food (e.g., unpasteurized dairy/soft cheese, deli/ready-to-eat meats, cantaloupe, sprouts), with survival of gastric acid and translocation across the gut epithelium then hematogenous spread. c) (1) Listeriolysin O (LLO) - pore-forming toxin enabling phagosomal escape. (2) ActA - surface protein driving host actin polymerization for intracellular motility and cell-to-cell spread (internalins InlA/InlB also acceptable). d) It lives intracellularly: LLO (with phospholipases PlcA/PlcB) lets it escape the phagosome and avoid lysosomal killing, and ActA-mediated actin-based motility propels it directly from cell to cell, so it is never exposed to antibodies, complement, or neutrophils in the extracellular space.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Listeria monocytogenes. Acquired: Foodborne - Consumption of unpasteurized cheeses/deli meats. Virulence factors: Listeriolysin O; Bacterial surface protein Act A; Siderophores. Immune evasion: Surface protein Act A allows the bacteria to propel itself against the cell membrane and form pseudopods which allows it to infect adjacent cells and evade the immune system; Listeriolysin O decreases T cell responsiveness and allows Listeria to avoid intracellular killing

questions.model_answer: a) Listeria monocytogenes. b) (1) Listeriolysin O (pore-forming toxin, phagosomal escape). (2) Internalin (InlA/InlB, binds E-cadherin/Met for host cell entry); ActA also acceptable. c) Its intracellular lifecycle: internalins mediate entry into host cells, LLO with phospholipases ruptures the phagosome so the organism escapes into the cytoplasm and divides, and ActA-driven actin polymerization propels it directly into adjacent cells, so it spreads without exposure to antibodies, complement, or neutrophils.

cohort_answer.text:
Listeria monocytogenes. Facultatively anaerobic, non-sporulating, catalase-positive, oxidase-negative, short, nonbranching, gram-positive rod that grows readily on blood agar, producing incomplete β-hemolysis, tumbling motility. Gram variable. 2 to 8% of cases of bacterial meningitis. Mortality of 15-29%. Neonates (less than 1mo), more than 60yo, alcoholics, cancer, steroids, other immunosuppressed patients and other conditions (DB, chronic renal disease, pregnancy, IBD, etc). HIV = low. Adults less than 50yo - screening. Outbreaks with contaminated food (coleslaw, vegetables, milk, cheese, etc).

B) Virulence factors: Internalin - a cell surface protein which interacts with E-cadherin, a receptor on epithelial cells and macrophages, resulting in the induction of phagocytosis. Listeriolysin O - once phagocytosed, the major virulence factor, listeriolysin O (a pore-forming toxin that induces T-cell receptor unresponsiveness), along with phospholipases, enables Listeria to escape from phagosomes and avoid intracellular killing. Act A - Bacterial surface protein necessary for induction of actin filament polymerization inside cell cytoplasm, propelling the bacteria to form filopods ingested by adjacent cells. Iron - important virulence factor; siderophores enable it to take iron from transferrin, enhancing organism growth.

C) Listeriolysin O enables Listeria to escape from phagosomes and avoid intracellular killing; once free in the cytoplasm the bacteria divide (doubling time ~1 hour) and, by inducing host cell actin polymerization (Act A), propel themselves to the cell membrane and move from cell to cell without being exposed to antibodies, complement, or neutrophils in the extracellular matrix.

parts.text: How does this organism evade the immune system?

parts_raw.text: D) How does this organism evade the immune system?

questions.model_answer: a) The organism is Listeria monocytogenes, a facultative intracellular pathogen whose principal immune-evasion strategy is an intracellular life cycle that avoids exposure to humoral defences: (1) Internalins A and B (InlA/InlB) bind host E-cadherin and Met to drive receptor-mediated endocytosis into non-phagocytic cells; (2) after uptake, listeriolysin O (LLO) together with phospholipases PlcA and PlcB lyse the phagosomal membrane, allowing escape into the cytosol and preventing lysosomal killing; (3) the surface protein ActA nucleates host actin into a comet tail that propels the organism directly into adjacent cells, so it spreads cell-to-cell without ever re-entering the extracellular space and evades antibody and complement. It also survives host defences during transit (bile-salt hydrolases and salt tolerance let it survive gastric/intestinal barriers).

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Meningitis/meningoencephalitis; (2) cerebritis or brain abscess; (3) rhombencephalitis (encephalitis of the cerebellum and brainstem). b) Ampicillin (or penicillin G) is the mainstay, with addition of an aminoglycoside (gentamicin) for synergy in severe/CNS infection; second-line trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or meropenem (cephalosporins must not be used). Treat Listeria meningitis for at least 21 days; focal infection such as brain abscess for 6-8 weeks. Corticosteroids should be stopped once L. monocytogenes is confirmed (associated with increased mortality). c) Any 3 of: Internalin A (InlA), Internalin B (InlB), listeriolysin O (LLO), phospholipases PlcA/PlcB, and ActA (actin-based motility).

cohort_answer.text: CNS infections: Rhomboencephalitis, cerebral abscess, meningitis. Treatment: IV ampicillin/gentamicin; alternative IV amp/septra if unable to use AG; other alternative septra/gent if unable to desensitize in PCN allergy; other alternatives meropenem/linezolid. Synergistic gentamicin for CNS/bacteremia/severe infection until clinical improvement or up to 3 weeks if tolerating well; avoid steroids (higher mortality). Duration: bacteremia 2 weeks (immunocompromised 3-6 weeks); CNS infection 3-4 weeks (immunocompromised 4-8 weeks); cerebritis/brain abscess 6-8 weeks (treat to radiologic resolution if imaging abnormal). Virulence factors: Listeriolysin O (porin formation); Internalin A; ActA (intracellular evasion, comet tail propulsion between cells); phospholipase; siderophores.
